title: The Five Habits
summary: Everything the opening asks of you, in five rules you can check against your own position every move.

sections.heading: Why rules instead of moves
sections.body: Nobody strong calculates the opening from scratch. They follow a small number of habits that reliably produce good positions, and deviate only when they see a concrete reason. If you know the rules but keep losing to people who know openings, the gap is usually not knowledge — it is that your opponent's habits are automatic and yours are not. Every principle below is something this app measures on your position after every move, which is why the feedback can tell you that your development stalled without knowing anything about the opening you are playing.

sections.heading: 1. Fight for the centre
sections.body: The four squares d4, e4, d5 and e5 are worth more than any others, because a piece in the centre touches more squares and can get anywhere quickly. Occupying them with pawns is the strongest form of control; attacking them with pieces from a distance is the flexible form. Both count. A knight on the rim touches four squares; the same knight in the centre touches eight.

diagram.caption: A normal Italian. Both sides have a pawn in the centre and every developed piece points at the four central squares.

sections.heading: 2. Develop every piece once, before you move any piece twice
sections.body: Each move you spend is a tempo, and moving the same piece repeatedly in the opening means the rest of your army is still asleep. There are exceptions — recapturing, escaping a real threat, or an actual tactic — but 'it looked more active over there' is not one of them. If you are about to move a developed piece while a knight or bishop is still on its starting square, you should be able to say out loud why.

sections.heading: 3. Castle early
sections.body: A king in the centre is the precondition for almost every disaster in this app's Tier 1 lessons. Every trap in the library works because a king was still on e1 or e8 when the files opened. Castling by move ten is not a superstition, it is what makes the tactics stop working. It also connects your rooks, which is the only way they ever join the game.

sections.heading: 4. Bring the queen out late
sections.body: The queen is the most valuable piece and therefore the easiest to attack. Every time an opponent develops a piece with an attack on your queen, they get a free move and you get nothing. This is the whole content of the Wayward Queen lesson: White's queen sortie is not refuted by a clever idea, it is refuted by developing normally and letting her be chased.

diagram.caption: 2.Qh5. Every black developing move from here also attacks or restricts the queen, so White is effectively playing a move behind.

sections.heading: 5. Do not block your own pieces
sections.body: The classic version is a bishop on d3 or e3 with the pawn still on d2 or e2 — the bishop stares at its own pawn for the next twenty moves. The general form is worth more than the specific one: before you place a piece, look at what is behind it and what it now cannot see. This app flags the central-pawn version automatically.

sections.heading: What to do with all this
sections.body: Read this once, then stop reading and start drilling. The habits only become automatic through the Test drills, where nobody tells you anything until you have already gone wrong. Start with the Tier 1 traps: they are the fastest way to make these five rules feel like consequences rather than commandments.
